{{Short description|Concept in differential geometry}}
In [[differential geometry]], a complete [[Riemannian manifold]] <math> (M,g) </math> is called a '''Ricci soliton''' if, and only if, there exists a smooth vector field <math> V </math> such that
:<math> \operatorname{Ric}(g) = \lambda \, g - \frac{1}{2} \mathcal{L}_V g, </math>
for some constant <math>\lambda \in \mathbb{R}</math>. Here <math>\operatorname{Ric}</math> is the [[Ricci curvature]] tensor and <math>\mathcal{L}</math> represents the [[Lie derivative]]. If there exists a function <math>f: M \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> such that <math> V = \nabla f </math> we call <math> (M,g) </math> a '''gradient Ricci soliton''' and the soliton equation becomes 
:<math> \operatorname{Ric}(g) + \nabla^2 f= \lambda \, g. </math>

Note that when <math>V = 0</math> or <math>f = 0</math> the above equations reduce to the Einstein equation. For this reason Ricci solitons are a generalization of [[Einstein manifold]]s.

== Self-similar solutions to Ricci flow == 
A Ricci soliton <math> (M,g_0) </math> yields a [[self-similar solution]] to the [[Ricci flow]] equation
:<math> \partial_t g_t = -2 \operatorname{Ric}(g_t).</math>
In particular, letting 
:<math>\sigma(t) := 1 - 2 \lambda t </math>
and integrating the time-dependent vector field <math>X(t) := \frac{1}{\sigma(t)} V</math> to give a family of diffeomorphisms <math>\Psi_t</math>, with <math>\Psi_0</math> the identity, yields a Ricci flow solution <math>(M, g_t)</math> by taking 
:<math> g_t = \sigma(t) \Psi^\ast_t(g_0).</math>
In this expression <math>\Psi^\ast_t(g_0)</math> refers to the [[pullback (differential geometry)|pullback]] of the metric <math>g_0</math> by the diffeomorphism <math>\Psi_t</math>. Therefore, up to [[diffeomorphism]] and depending on the sign of <math>\lambda</math>, a Ricci soliton homothetically shrinks, remains steady or expands under Ricci flow.

==Examples of Ricci solitons==
===Shrinking (<math> \lambda > 0 </math>)===
* Gaussian shrinking soliton <math> (\mathbb{R}^n, g_{eucl}, f(x) = \frac{\lambda}{2}|x|^2)</math>
* Shrinking round sphere <math> S^n, n \geq 2 </math>
* Shrinking round cylinder <math> S^{n-1} \times \R, n \geq 3 </math>
* The four dimensional FIK shrinker (discovered by [[M. Feldman]], [[Tom Ilmanen|T. Ilmanen]], [[D. Knopf]]) <ref name=":0">{{citation

*Expanding Kähler-Ricci solitons on the [[complex line]] bundles <math>O(-k), k>n</math> over <math>\mathbb{C}P^n, n \geq 1</math>.<ref name=":0" />
*Einstein manifolds of negative scalar curvature

== Singularity models in Ricci flow ==
Shrinking and steady Ricci solitons are fundamental objects in the study of [[Ricci flow]] as they appear as blow-up limits of [[Ricci flow#Singularities|singularities]]. In particular, it is known that all Type I singularities are modeled on non-collapsed gradient shrinking Ricci solitons.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Enders | first1=Joerg
| last2=Müller | first2=Reto
| last3=Topping | first3=Peter M.
| title=On Type I Singularities in Ricci flow
| journal=Communications in Analysis and Geometry
| volume=19
| issue=5
| date=2011
| pages=905–922
| doi=10.4310/CAG.2011.v19.n5.a4 | doi-access=free| hdl=10044/1/10485
| hdl-access=free
| arxiv=1005.1624
}}</ref> Type II singularities are expected to be modeled on steady Ricci solitons in general, however to date this has not been proven, even though all known examples are.

==Soliton Identities==
Taking the trace of the Ricci soliton equation <math> Ric + \frac12 \mathcal{L}_V g = \lambda g</math> gives
{{NumBlk|:|<math> S + \operatorname{div} V = \lambda n </math>, |{{EqRef|1}}}}
where <math>S</math> is the [[scalar curvature]] and <math>n = \operatorname{dim} M </math>.
By taking the divergence of the Ricci soliton equation and invoking the [[contracted Bianchi identities]] and {{EqNote|1}}, it follows that
:<math> \Delta V + \operatorname{Ric} \circ V = 0 \quad \text{or equivalently, in components,} \quad \Delta V_i + \operatorname{Ric}_{ij} V^j = 0. </math>


For gradient Ricci solitons <math>V = \nabla f</math>, similar arguments show
:<math> S + \Delta f = \lambda n \quad \text{and} \quad  \nabla ( S + | \nabla f|^2 - 2 \lambda f ) = 0.</math> 
In particular, if <math>M</math> is connected, then there exists a constant <math>C</math> such that
:<math> S + |\nabla f|^2 = 2 \lambda f + C. </math>
Often, in the shrinking or expanding cases (<math> \lambda \ne 0 </math>), <math> f</math> is replaced by <math> f - \frac C{2 \lambda} </math> to obtain a gradient Ricci soliton normalized such that <math> S + |\nabla f|^2 = 2 \lambda f</math>.
